Dossier

Raise the bar.

Research on leadership points to four things that make a team more ambitious, and one warning about using them too hard. This dossier gives you the evidence, the sentences and the grammar to talk about it.

Tap or hover any highlighted phrase or dotted word to see it in Portuguese.

Talk about these first

Then read the article and see who agrees with you.

  1. Think of a boss, teacher or coach who made you try something you thought was too hard. What did that person do?
    “My first manager expected me to present to a client in my second month. I was nervous, but she let me prepare with her, and she made me practice twice. It worked.”
  2. Has someone ever given you a target that felt impossible? What happened?
    “Last year we had to double our sales in six months. Nobody explained why. We missed it, and people stopped trying after the second month.”
  3. Who should set a team’s targets: the leader, the team, or both? Why?
    “Both. I would ask the team to propose a number first. Then I would add a little more, and I would explain why.”
  4. Your manager says: “We need to be more ambitious.” What do you want to hear next? What do you not want to hear?
    “I want to hear why, and what support I will get. I do not want to hear ‘Just work harder.’”
  5. Can a team be too ambitious? How would you know?
    “Yes. If people are tired, if they hide bad news, or if everybody expects to fail, the goal is too far for now.”
Leadership · Teams

Four levers and one warning

A team does not become ambitious because the leader asks for more. Research points to four things leaders do, and one way to overdo it.

By EIC Magazine · 5 min read · Hover over the dotted words to see them in Portuguese

Listen to the article0:00
Speed
The recording is not on this page yet.

Almost every manager says, “I want an ambitious team.” Fewer managers ask what they should do to build one. That matters: Gallup says managers account for 70% of the variance in team engagement. Decades of research on goals, expectations and teamwork point to four levers: meaning, belief, targets and safety. They also point to a warning: a stretch goal can hurt a team if the leader uses it badly.

Meaning

People work harder for a goal they believe in. In a review of 35 years of research on goal setting, Edwin Locke and Gary Latham found that commitment grows when leaders communicate an inspiring vision and behave supportively. A 2004 analysis of 87 sources found that transformational leadership, the style that inspires people around a vision, was linked to better outcomes, and that hands-off leadership was linked to worse ones. In a 2025 article in Harvard Business Review, Adam Galinsky described inspiring leaders as visionary, exemplar and mentor. The mentor, he wrote, challenges people to become the best version of themselves.

Belief

What a leader expects often becomes what a team delivers. This is called the Pygmalion effect. In a 2000 review of 17 studies and 2,874 people, D. Brian McNatt found a strong average effect of managers’ expectations on performance, but the effect varied a lot from one setting to another. A classic Harvard Business Review article by J. Sterling Livingston gives managers a short instruction: expect the best. In practice, that means you expect people to reach a high standard, and you say so.

Targets

Belief needs a number. Locke and Latham found that specific, difficult goals consistently led to higher performance than urging people to do their best. The effect is strongest when people are committed to the goal, and people also need feedback on their progress. Google asks teams to set ambitious objectives that “may feel somewhat uncomfortable,” then scores them. The score shows how much of each objective the team reached: 100% is all of it. An average score of 60 to 70 percent is the sweet spot. A higher score may mean the goal was not high enough. Joseph Folkman adds that the best leaders use both pull and push: they give people a say and inspire them, and they also hold people accountable.

Safety

A hard goal asks people to risk failing. In Google’s study of 180 teams, the first of five dynamics was psychological safety. Amy Edmondson defines it as “a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.” On a safe team, a person can say “I am stuck” or “this will not work” without fear. Progress also matters. Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer wrote in Harvard Business Review that making progress in meaningful work contributes more to a positive inner work life than anything else they examined. Their advice to managers: help people take a step forward every day.

The warning

Stretch goals also fail. In “The Stretch Goal Paradox” (Harvard Business Review, 2017), Sim Sitkin, Chet Miller and Kelly See wrote that companies in trouble often adopt stretch goals in a desperate attempt to turn things around, and nearly always fail. The companies that could benefit most, those with recent wins and spare resources, rarely use them. Another review, “Goals Gone Wild,” listed the side effects of too many goals: unethical behavior, too much focus on one area, a damaged culture and lower intrinsic motivation. Its authors say goals should be prescribed in doses, not as a standard remedy. A 2025 study of early-career engineers adds a question of fairness: stretch assignments did not benefit every group equally.

So the question for every leader is the same: what are you asking the team to do, and what will you do when the team falls short?

“We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.”John F. Kennedy, Rice University, 12 September 1962

4Chunks

Chunks and patterns

Leaders repeat the same phrases. Learn the whole phrase and the pattern that goes with it, and the sentence builds itself.

Three families you already know

Three of the phrases below are verb patterns. The first verb decides what comes next, and these are the same Families 1, 2 and 3 from the Verb Patterns lesson.

FamilyThe patternThe verbsExample
1verb + person + to + verbask · expect · challenge · encourage · invite · trust · push · remind · want · need · would like“We encourage people to speak up.”
2let · make · have + person + verbOnly three verbs. No to after the person.“Let the team decide the deadline.”
3suggest · recommend · propose · insist + that + person + verbFormal. The verb stays in the base form: that he go, that they meet.“I propose that we meet every Monday.”

Where the not goes

FamilyWhere the not goesExample
1Two places“I didn’t ask them to start.” × “I asked them not to start.”
2The first verb“I didn’t let them start.” Never “I let them not start.”
3After that“I suggest that they not start.” Never “that they don’t start.”

7The case

Set the goal in five moves

Say why it matters. Give a specific, difficult target. Show that you believe in the team. Make bad news safe. Say how you will score it.

  1. 1Say why it matters

    Here is why this matters: our clients wait two days for an answer, and some of them leave.

    Start with the reason, not with the number.

  2. 2Give a specific, difficult target

    I’d like us to cut the response time from 48 hours to 24 by the end of the year.

    A number and a date. “Do your best” is not a target.

  3. 3Show that you believe in the team

    This is a stretch, and I expect you to find ways that I have not thought of.

    Belief is part of the message. Say it.

  4. 4Make bad news safe

    I want you to tell me early if we are falling behind. Nobody will be blamed for bad news.

    Say what will happen when someone brings a problem.

  5. 5Say how you will score it

    Reaching 70% will count as a strong result, and we will review it together every month.

    Say what success and a miss look like.

Too blunt, say this

Say the better version out loud first. Then tap to check.

Just work harder.What would it take to reach this target?
I don’t want to hear excuses.Tell me what is getting in the way, and I will see what I can take off your plate.
You have no ambition.Where do you want to grow this year?
Failure is not an option.We may fall short. I want us to find out early.
If you miss it, it’s on you.If we miss it, we will look at it together.
Your turn · the case

Choose one goal for a team you lead or know. Make your case in five moves, out loud, in under one minute.

“Here is why this matters: new customers wait a week to get an answer from us. I’d like us to reduce that to three days by December. I expect you to find ways that I have not thought of. I want you to tell me early if we are falling behind, and nobody will be blamed for bad news. Three days will be the goal, and four will still count as a good result.”
8The answer

When the team says it cannot be done

Do not argue. Hear the worry, limit the claim, ask what it would take, and offer something real.

  1. 1Hear the worry

    I hear you, and it is a big step.

    Say what you understand before you say what you want.

  2. 2Limit the claim

    That may be true for the full year. Let’s start with the first three months.

    A claim about “always” is almost always wrong.

  3. 3Ask what it would take

    What would it take to get there?

    A calm question works better than a speech.

  4. 4Offer something real

    I can’t add people, but I can take the weekly report off your plate.

    A small, true offer is better than a big promise.

  5. 5Set a checkpoint

    Let’s review it in four weeks and adjust if we need to.

    People accept a hard goal more easily when it has a review date.

A real exchange

Analyst

Forty percent more? That is not realistic. Last year we missed by thirty.

Manager

I hear you, and it is a big jump. What would it take to get there?

Analyst

Two more people, or fewer reports.

Manager

Fair point. I can’t add people, but I can take the weekly report off your plate. Can we review it in four weeks?

When the director pushes back

Director

If the team is not a little afraid, it will not push.

Manager

I see your point, but Google’s study of 180 teams ranked psychological safety first of five. What does the evidence say about fear?

Your turn · analyst

The analyst says: “This goal is not realistic. Last year we missed by 30%.” Answer in three moves: hear the worry, ask what it would take, set a checkpoint.

“I hear you, and last year was hard. What would it take to get there this year? Let’s review it in four weeks and adjust if we need to.”
Your turn · director

The director says: “Nobody works hard when they feel safe.” Answer in three moves: agree with what you can, limit the claim, ask for the evidence.

“I see your point, some pressure helps. But that may not be true for every team: in Google’s study of 180 teams, psychological safety came first. What does the evidence say about fear?”
9Other side

How the team hears it

Your team does not read your plan. It listens for answers to a few questions: why this goal, does my boss believe I can do it, what happens if I miss. Here is the evidence behind each question and the words you can use.

Google’s scale for an ambitious objective

Each objective is scored from 0 to 1, shown here as 0 to 100%. The score is the share of the objective the team reached: 100% means all of it. Google re:Work, Set goals with OKRs.

What the team asks, and what the evidence says

LeverThe team asksThe evidence
Meaning“Why this goal?”Commitment grows when leaders communicate an inspiring vision and behave supportively. Locke and Latham, 2002.
Belief“Does my boss think I can do it?”Managers’ expectations were linked to performance in a review of 17 studies. The effect varied a lot. McNatt, 2000.
Target“What exactly, and by when?”Specific, difficult goals led to higher performance than “do your best”. Locke and Latham, 2002.
Safety“What happens if I miss?”Psychological safety came first of five dynamics in Google’s study of 180 teams.
Dose“How many goals, and how hard?”Companies in trouble adopt stretch goals and nearly always fail. Sitkin, Miller and See, Harvard Business Review, 2017. Goals should be prescribed in doses.
Fairness“Who gets the big projects, and who gets the credit?”Stretch assignments did not benefit every group equally. Gilmartin and others, Harvard Business Review, 2025.

Six terms and the sentence for the meeting

TermIn the meeting
stretch goal n.“Let’s treat this as a stretch goal: 70% will count as a strong result.”
buy-in n.“I want your buy-in before I take this to the director.”
commitment n.“A hard goal only works if the team has real commitment to it.”
psychological safety n.“Psychological safety means you can say ‘this will not work’ in this room.”
accountability n.“Accountability is not blame: we all know who owns what.”
milestone n.“Let’s set a milestone for each month, so we can see progress.”

11Glossary

Watch out, then look it up

False friends

WordFrom the PortugueseWhat it really means
realizerealizarIt means to notice or understand. For a goal, say reach or achieve. Say: We reached the target.
attendatenderIt means to go to an event. For a target, say meet. For a client, say help or serve.
assumeassumirIt means to suppose something is true. For responsibility, say take responsibility. Say: I take responsibility for the plan.
pretendpretenderIt means to fake something. For a plan, say intend to. Say: We intend to double the target.
compromisecompromissoA compromise is an agreement in which each side gives something up. For a duty or a promise, say commitment.
supportsuportarIt means to help. For something hard to bear, say handle or stand. Say: He cannot handle the pressure.
